Project Title: Garden of Sounds

Garden of Sounds is a browser-based interactive soundscape where toddlers explore music by tapping and moving illustrated garden objects. These eight parallel prototypes examine how simple spatial controls and visual feedback can communicate the relationship between a child’s actions and the sounds they produce. Rather than presenting a completed interface, each prototype isolates a specific interaction choice for comparison during peer user testing.

Area 1: Mapping — Garden of Sounds

The first area explores how the position of a draggable object can control sound through the extended technique of space. The three prototypes move from separated pitch zones to continuous pitch control and two-dimensional sound control. These variations examine how simple spatial relationships can allow toddlers to change musical properties without needing written instructions or formal musical knowledge.

Prototype 1: Three pitch zones (opens in a new tab)

The canvas is divided into three illustrated height zones: underground, garden and sky. Placing the object in a different zone produces a note from a matching low, middle or high register. Controlled randomness introduces small variations within each register while keeping the relationship between height and pitch understandable.
Drag the flower into the sky, garden, or underground, then release it to play a note from that zone.

Prototype 2: Continuous vertical pitch (opens in a new tab)

This prototype removes the separate zones and maps the object’s vertical position directly to sound frequency. Moving the object upward gradually raises the pitch, while moving it downward lowers it. This design explores whether a continuous relationship between movement and sound provides more direct musical control.
Drag the flower up and down to change its pitch continuously. The display shows the current frequency in hertz.

Prototype 3: Note and Octave Mapping (opens in a new tab)

This prototype extends the spatial mapping across both axes and introduces two draggable objects. Vertical movement selects notes from C to B, while horizontal movement selects octaves 1 to 8. Combining note and octave mapping with layered repeating sounds provides greater control while maintaining the simple action of moving an object.
Move the sound objects vertically to select notes from C to B, and horizontally to move between octaves 1 and 8. Press Play Garden to start the sound.

Area 2: Feedback — Garden of Sounds

The second area explores how visual feedback can communicate the result and continuing state of a musical interaction. The five prototypes compare feedback attached to the object, feedback appearing within the environment, and movement connected to continuing sound. These variations support cause-and-effect learning by helping toddlers recognise when their actions have produced or changed a sound.

Prototype 4: Object movement feedback (opens in a new tab)

Tapping the object produces a sound while making it briefly grow and bounce. The movement creates an immediate response at the same location as the user’s action. This direct connection is intended to make the result of each tap visible without adding text or additional controls.
Tap the flower to play a note and watch it grow and bounce in time with the sound.

Prototype 5: Colour and glow feedback (opens in a new tab)

Tapping the object changes its colour and creates a temporary glow while playing the sound. This prototype uses light and colour rather than physical movement to confirm the interaction. The response keeps the object recognisable while making its active state more visually noticeable.
Tap the flower to play a note and see its colour brighten as soft glow waves fade away.

Prototype 6: Environmental ripple feedback (opens in a new tab)

In this prototype, tapping the object creates ripples across the garden while briefly deepening the background colour. Moving the feedback beyond the object makes the wider storybook environment feel connected to the sound. This design supports the project’s framing as an interactive garden rather than a conventional musical control panel.
Tap the flower to play a note and watch ripples spread across the garden as its background briefly deepens in colour.

Prototype 7: Playing-state feedback (opens in a new tab)

Tapping the object once starts a repeating sound and makes the object rotate slowly. Tapping it again stops both the sound and the movement. Unlike the earlier temporary responses, the continuous spinning communicates that the object remains active after the first interaction.
Tap the flower to start a repeating sound and continuous rotation, then tap it again to stop both.

Prototype 8: Rhythm feedback (opens in a new tab)

Tapping the object starts a repeating sound, while the object briefly shakes from side to side with every musical note. The visual movement is synchronised with the rhythm rather than continuing at a fixed speed. This design explores whether repeated visual responses can communicate both the playing state and the timing of the sound.
